overview: Veterinary technologists and technicians are the nurses of animal care. Under a veterinarian's direction, they run lab tests, take X-rays, give anesthesia, assist in surgery, monitor recovering animals and keep drug logs. O*NET rates knowledge of medicine at 4.14 out of 5 for this job and biology at 3.99. Most complete a 2-year accredited program, 26% report an associate degree in O*NET data, and pass a national exam. The BLS May 2025 median is $47,380 across 129,140 jobs. The work means long hours on your feet and exposure to infection and animal bites.
pay: Vet techs earn a median of $47,380, and the top 10% earn $63,180 or more. The District of Columbia, California and Washington have the highest state medians, from $59,740 to $61,270. Texas has the most jobs, 16,730, at a median of $39,410, while Louisiana pays the least at $35,530.

faq.q: How much do vet techs make?
faq.a: The BLS May 2025 median is $47,380 a year. The middle half earn between $38,910 and $57,650. The District of Columbia ($61,270) and California ($60,630) pay the most, while Mississippi ($36,380) and Louisiana ($35,530) have the lowest state medians. Specialty and emergency hospitals often pay more.

faq.q: How do you become a vet tech?
faq.a: Most complete a 2-year associate degree program accredited by the American Veterinary Medical Association, then pass the national VTNE exam and a state credential. In O*NET data, 26% hold an associate degree and 41% a high school diploma. There are 2 related programs.

faq.q: Is being a vet tech hard?
faq.a: It is demanding. In O*NET data, vet techs rank above 91% of U.S. jobs for working more than 40 hours a week, and long hours on your feet are common. You handle frightened animals and face exposure to infection, so cautiousness matters.

faq.q: What can vet techs do next?
faq.a: Surgical Assistants are an 84% match and earn $66,800, 41% more. Respiratory Therapists are a 78% match and earn $82,280, 74% more, according to BLS May 2025 data. Both use the same clinical skills with people instead of animals, after an associate degree program.
